summary.text: Augustus, born Gaius Octavius and also called Octavian, founded the Roman Empire and was its first emperor from 27 BC until his death in AD 14.
Named heir by his great-uncle Julius Caesar, he ruled after his side beat Mark Antony at Actium, keeping the look of a free republic while holding control of the army.
His reign began an era of imperial peace, and he enlarged the empire, reformed taxes and currency, and built roads and a standing army.

facts.label: Heir of
facts.value: Named primary heir in Julius Caesar's will

facts.label: Victory at Actium
facts.value: 31 BC, won with naval commander Marcus Agrippa

facts.label: Successor
facts.value: His stepson and adoptive son Tiberius

items.prompt: After the civil wars, Rome keeps its Senate, elected magistrates and assemblies. What let one man hold autocratic power regardless?

options.label: Command of most armies and half the provinces
Yearly re-election as consul
A crown granted by the assemblies
Ownership of the Senate's treasury

items.explain: He controlled the military and half of Rome's provinces, so he kept autocratic power behind the republic's outward form.

items.prompt: To avoid looking like a king, he stopped standing for election as consul. What did the Senate give him instead?

options.label: The crown and the title of dictator
The powers of the tribunate and censorship, plus titles
A permanent place as one of two consuls
Command of the Senate's own private army

items.explain: The Senate granted him the powers of the tribunate and censorship and titles such as princeps, augustus and pater patriae.

items.prompt: Three allies shared power after Caesar's assassins lost at Philippi. How did that partnership end?

options.label: It became a lasting rule of three
All three retired in favour of the Senate
Rivalry split it; one was exiled, another beaten
Two of them drove the third from Rome

items.explain: Competing ambitions tore the alliance apart: Lepidus was exiled and Antony was defeated at Actium.

items.prompt: Historians call the same man Octavian for his early career and Augustus later. What explains the switch?

options.label: He chose the new name himself when he became consul
His father's name replaced his mother's
Historians use it only for his boyhood
In 27 BC the Senate granted him the honorific 'the revered'

items.explain: Historians usually say Octavian for 44 to 27 BC and Augustus from 27 BC, when the Senate granted him that honorific.

items.prompt: Rather than fight on every border, how did he protect the empire's edges?

options.label: A continuous wall of forts along each frontier
A buffer region of client states plus peace treaties
Annual tribute paid to every neighbouring king
Moving the capital to the frontier

items.explain: He secured the empire with a buffer region of client states and negotiated peace treaties with the Parthian Empire and the Kingdom of Kush.

items.prompt: A blaze spreads through a Roman neighbourhood in his reign. What new body could respond?

options.label: An official fire-fighting service for the city
Volunteer crews paid by the Senate
Legions summoned from the provinces
Temple priests under the supreme pontiff

items.explain: Among his reforms he established official police and fire-fighting services for the city of Rome.

paragraphs.heading: The first emperor
paragraphs.text: Augustus, born Gaius Octavius and also known as Octavian, founded the Roman Empire and ruled as its first emperor from 27 BC until he died in AD 14. His reign opened an era of imperial peace, the Pax Romana, when the Roman world was mostly free of war, and it also began an imperial cult. Under him Rome took up the principate, a way of governing in which the emperor showed outward respect to the Senate. That system lasted until the Crisis of the Third Century.

paragraphs.heading: Childhood and schooling
paragraphs.text: He was born on 23 September 63 BC on a family property on Rome's Palatine Hill. His father came from a moderately wealthy equestrian family, and his mother, Atia, was a niece of Julius Caesar. His first public appearance was the speech at the funeral of his grandmother Julia, Caesar's sister. A Greek slave tutor named Sphaerus taught him reading, writing, arithmetic and Greek. As a teenager he studied philosophy and both Latin and Greek rhetoric with several teachers.

paragraphs.heading: Caesar's heir
paragraphs.text: Caesar, his great-uncle, named him main heir in his will, and after Caesar was murdered in 44 BC Octavian took over his estate and his name. He fought to win the loyalty of Caesar's legions, and in 43 BC he marched on Rome and became its youngest elected consul. With Mark Antony and Marcus Lepidus he formed a triumvirate, a regime with legal power to outlaw and fight Caesar's killers and their allies. After winning at Philippi in 42 BC, the three divided the Republic among themselves and ruled as oligarchs in practice.

paragraphs.heading: Sole master of Rome
paragraphs.text: Rival ambitions broke the alliance apart. Octavian had Lepidus exiled in 36 BC, and his naval commander Marcus Agrippa beat Antony at the Battle of Actium in Greece in 31 BC. Antony and Cleopatra, his wife and the Ptolemaic queen of Egypt, killed themselves as Octavian invaded Egypt, which then became his personal property.

paragraphs.heading: A republic on the surface
paragraphs.text: Augustus made a deal with the rest of Rome's elite: he would keep up the look of a free republic, built around the Senate, the magistrates and the assemblies. In practice his grip on the army and on half the provinces gave him the power of an autocrat. To avoid seeming a king or dictator he eventually stopped running for consul, yet the Senate gave him the powers of tribune and censor and titles such as princeps ("first citizen") and pater patriae ("father of the country"). It even named the month of August after him, and when Lepidus died he became pontifex maximus, the "supreme pontiff".

paragraphs.heading: Building an empire
paragraphs.text: Augustus greatly enlarged the empire, taking Egypt, Dalmatia, Pannonia, Noricum and Raetia and completing the conquest of Hispania, though he met a major setback in Germania. Beyond the borders he set up a buffer of client states and made peace treaties with the Parthian Empire and the Kingdom of Kush. He reformed taxes and currency, built road networks with an official courier service and created a standing professional army. In Rome he set up the Praetorian Guard and police and fire services, and he renovated much of the city.

paragraphs.heading: Names and death
paragraphs.text: His names tracked his rise: by 38 BC he had swapped "Gaius" for the victory title imperator, "commander", and in 27 BC the Senate named him Augustus, "the revered". He wrote, and he supported poets such as Virgil. He died of natural causes in AD 14 at 75, and the Senate declared him a god after his death, though rumors long held that his wife Livia poisoned him. His stepson and adopted son Tiberius followed him as emperor.
